_note: Hand-written by the pilot's builder after the final scoring run of 14 November 2026. If the data changes, reread every sentence here against out/results.json.
caveat: Published replications report that language-model panels give effects two to three times the human size, and report an effect in most studies where people showed none.
panel_note: All five classic controls came out in the direction known from people, and no null pair crossed the half-point floor. The floor is doing real work. One null pair, which changes only the colour of a van, differs by 0.30 points with an interval that excludes zero, so a rule based on significance alone would have reported a false effect. Judged by haiku alone, or by sonnet alone, two of the five null pairs would have crossed the floor; judged by opus or fable alone, none would.
Comprehension is at its ceiling, so on a model panel that component barely separates pairs. All six wrong answers came from haiku judges, and five of the six were on my own control pairs.
headline: **The pipeline runs end to end and its own checks pass.** 1,200 judgments from 40 fresh-context judges, every batch complete, and the transcripts show that no judge used any tool, so none could have looked up a factor or a prediction.

**Direction was easy, size was harder.** 17 of 20 authored pairs split in the predicted direction and 13 of 20 also landed in the predicted size bin. Earlier work on models predicting experiments found the same pattern.

**Only two of the five factors separate good pairs from bad.** Intention vs. accident and knowledge vs. luck gave gaps of 2.3 to 4.4 points for every author, so a correct prediction of a large gap there says little about the author. The misses came from doing vs. allowing (gaps of 0.2 to 0.8, one of them reversed) and from norm violation and causation (0.35 to 1.9).

**Authors reached for the same scenes.** 8 of the 20 pairs share a setting with another author's pair or with one of my controls: two rival caterers whose freezer is switched off, two greenhouses left to the frost, three farm gates left open, and an overloaded circuit. The originality audit grades each pair alone and missed all of it. No pair was graded as fresh.

**The auditors catch gross problems and cannot rank subtle ones.** They flagged 12 of 12 planted confounds, recognised 19 of 20 classic paraphrases and raised no false alarm on the null pairs. On the authored pairs any two of them gave the same confound grade only about half the time (52.5%) and the same originality grade less often (43.3%). The order among the 13 pairs that hit both direction and size (composites from 77 to 93) is therefore mostly audit noise.

**The audit let a broken pair into the top four.** In the opus author's moral-luck pair the harm does not follow from the lapse it is meant to follow from. One auditor of four caught it. The card below has the details.

**Same-model effects are visible even inside one vendor.** Judges produced larger gaps on pairs written by their own model than on other authors' pairs (2.25 against 1.81 points, larger on 15 of 20 pairs). The fable auditor graded fable-written pairs as almost free of confounds (0.2) and other authors' pairs at 1.3. The other three auditors also found the fable pairs cleaner than average, so some of that may be deserved, but five pairs cannot separate merit from self-preference. The builder of this pilot is also a Claude model, so the same caution applies to the builder's own controls and flags.
author_note: Sonnet's five predictions were all right on direction and size. Haiku wrote the loosest pairs, with 31 words changed on average and the highest confound grades, and got one of five fully right. Fable's pairs drew the lowest confound grades, with the self-preference caveat above. These are five pairs per author on one panel; they are not a ranking of models.
controls_note: **The classic controls reproduce, but the panel may simply know them.** Auditors named the source of 19 of 20 paraphrases. A judge that recognises the pen case can report the textbook answer without having the intuition, so 5 of 5 here is weaker evidence than it looks. Where a checked human number exists on a comparable scale, the panel is in range. People rated “Professor Smith caused the problem” at 5.2 of 7 in the original pen study; this panel gave 4.65 in the matching version. In people, a bad outcome raised blame for the same negligence by 0.33 to 0.39 standard deviations; this panel's gap on the brakes story is 0.60 points, or 0.61 standard deviations, because its ratings vary less than people's do.

**All five references were checked against the papers on 15 November.** Four are checked from the papers themselves, two of those from copies the project owner supplied after the sites refused automated access. The pen case rests on a later paper by one of its authors that reports the original numbers. Several descriptions first written from memory were wrong: the car study's headline was that East and South Asian participants mostly did attribute knowledge; the coffee study measured permissibility in ten people, not blame; and in the moral-luck study wrongness moved about as much as blame. **Three controls have no human data for the exact contrast used here:** the clear-knowledge version of the car case and the “professor is allowed” version of the pen case are my own, and the human numbers for the brakes case come from other negligence stories. For those three, “reproduced” means the expected direction appeared, not that a measured human gap was matched.

**My own controls are not clean.** Auditors gave all five classic pairs a confound grade of 1. The pens control had the lowest comprehension of all 30 pairs: three of five haiku judges misread the rule in the version where faculty may not take pens. Dropping the wrong answers moves that control's gap from 1.70 to 1.90 points, so the conclusion holds, but the wording (“supposed to buy their own”) should be made plainer before reuse.

**The planted confounds were blatant.** All four auditors graded all three at the maximum. That shows auditors catch a gross confound; it says nothing about subtle ones, and the low agreement on real pairs suggests they do not.
diagnostics_note: Opus and fable are close to deterministic at this setting: in more than half of the scenarios all five repeats gave the same rating. Five repeats of such a model are not five independent readings, so the main interval is narrower than the evidence warrants. That is why a gap also has to reach half a point and appear in at least three of the four models before it counts.
vendor_note: **First place depends on the panel.** Two pairs decide it. On Sonnet's doing-vs-allowing pair, Claude finds the small gap Sonnet predicted and Gemini finds none. On Fable's norm-violation pair it is the reverse. Both are small effects close to the 0.5-point line, where model panels are least reliable.

**Which panel to believe on those two pairs is open.** On public human data, when one vendor confirmed a gap and the other did not, people backed the Claude-only gaps 0 times out of 9 and the Gemini-only gaps 16 times out of 26. That leans toward Gemini's reading, and so toward Fable first, but those were different stories. Requiring both vendors to agree did not help there: people backed 8 of 19 such gaps. See `reports/Calibration on public human data.md`.
**Doing vs allowing is the least stable factor.** The panels disagree on three of its four authored pairs, and on the size of the classic control. Haiku is last under every scoring.
persona_note: **Personas move first place too.** Sonnet's lead rested on two pairs with small gaps. With personas its doing-vs-allowing pair shows no gap, as with Gemini, and its moral-luck pair is no longer confirmed. Fable's norm-violation pair still shows none. Fable leads under the Gemini panel, the two-vendor scoring and the persona panel; Sonnet leads under the original panel and the six-model average, which is mostly Claude. Only Haiku's place, last, holds under all of them.

**Persona judges are more cautious about small effects.** On public human data that made them more accurate, cutting false confirmations. Here it also costs one real effect: the classic moral-luck control, which people do show, is no longer confirmed.

au_fable_moral_luck: **Right on the line, which the original score missed.** Blame rose from 4.40 when the sparks died on the gravel to 5.90 when they burned the shed: a gap of 1.50, on the boundary between a small and a large effect. Under the original rule that fell a hair short of “large” and cost a quarter of the prediction score; under the distance rule it gets full credit, which is the kind of case the change was for. All four judge models moved the same way, haiku least (0.6).

Its weaknesses: the author expected about 3 for the harmless version and the panel gave 4.4, so the panel blamed the risky decision itself more than predicted. One auditor pointed out that the question names no object, so readers of the harmless version must guess what the blame is for. The harmful version also adds “and all the tools inside it”. The structure is the standard negligence-and-outcome case behind Nagel's drivers, and originality was graded 1 or 2.
au_haiku_knowledge_luck: **A large effect, predicted as a small one.** The author expected a small gap because many readers call a luckily true belief knowledge. The panel gave 6.00 against 1.95, a gap of 4.05, the largest of the four knowledge pairs, and all four judge models agreed. The original rule gave 0.75 for the right direction and a neighbouring size class; the distance rule gives nothing for a prediction that ends 2.5 points short of the measured gap.

The pair also tells the reader the answer. The lucky version states outright that “the beep had nothing to do with the crate” and adds that nobody repaired the scanner, a negligence cue; the other version adds certified, perfect reliability. Three auditors graded the confounds 1 and one graded them 2, and three of four flagged the question, “How well did Priya know…”, as presupposing knowledge. The mechanism is Russell's stopped clock with a scanner. Whether people would show the smaller gap the author expected is a question for the human run: studies of knowledge attribution in people are mixed.
au_fable_intent_accident: **What works.** Ten words change. The act is the same, on the same freezer, and version B is a real mistake and not a different story. Blame falls from 6.9 to 3.75 and every model agrees. B stays well above the floor because readers hold Mara responsible for not checking which freezer she switched off, which is the right residue for an accident.

**What to hold against it.** It is on the easiest factor: every author got a gap above 3 points here. The sonnet author independently wrote the same story, a rival caterer's wedding desserts thawed in a shared kitchen, so an originality grade of 2 is generous. Version A sits at the ceiling of the scale, which caps the measurable gap. Its lead over the field is a single confound grade on which the auditors disagree: the haiku auditor gave it 2, because B hands Mara a harmless purpose as well as a false belief. And the zero came in part from an auditor of the author's own model.
au_sonnet_moral_luck: **What works.** The tightest pair in the set: seven words change, the choice is identical, and the risk is stated as a number (one time in twenty), so a reader cannot infer a different risk from the outcome. All four auditors found no confound. The gap is 0.85 points, where the author said it would be, in all four models.

**What to hold against it.** It is a stock negligence case in the Nagel family, close in shape to my own classic control, and the auditors graded its originality 1 or 2. A small gap is also the hardest kind to trust on this panel: 0.85 is less than twice the noise floor.
au_opus_moral_luck: **It scores well and should not.** Gus's rule is to check the fridge thermometer before he locks up. In version A the switch trips during the night, after he has left. Checking would have shown a working fridge, so skipping the check changed nothing. The pair does not show one risk turning out well or badly; it shows a lapse followed by an unrelated accident.

The panel still blamed him 1.85 points more in the harmful version, which says as much about the judges as about the pair. Only the fable auditor caught the flaw and graded it 2; the others gave 1, 1 and 0, and the rule recorded 1. The versions also differ by 21 words, with a storm, a power surge and two hospitalised customers on one side only.
au_sonnet_intent_accident: **What works.** A gap of 3.5 points, as predicted, in all four models.

**What went wrong.** The versions differ in more than intention. A gives Dana a motive of commercial gain; B gives her an errand, and adds that she “does not notice the freezer is running”, which invites a reading of carelessness. Three of four auditors flagged the change of motive. It is the same story as the fable author's pair, and version A is at the ceiling of the scale.
au_fable_norm_causation: **No usable gap.** A four-word change with no confound produced 0.35 points, and only two of four models showed it at all (fable 1.2, opus 0.4, haiku 0, sonnet slightly negative). The largest gap came from the author's own model.

**Why.** First, it is the pen case with a shelf: two people each add one of two jointly sufficient contributions and only one of them is permitted. Every auditor named Knobe and Fraser, and one graded originality 0. Second, the author made the mechanism symmetrical and physical (two 20-kilogram boxes, neither person knowing the limit), which invites the answer “half each” whatever the notice says. The author's own rationale expected some readers to do exactly that.
au_opus_doing_allowing: **A clean pair that moved nobody.** Five words change and the ratings are 5.65 against 5.45. Jonah knows about the frost, wants the cool air and could shut the window in seconds in both versions, so readers blame him heavily either way. The author's rationale predicted this compression and predicted a small gap regardless.

This is the failure the benchmark exists to catch: a controlled pair whose factor does not move this panel. It may be a fact about the factor and not the author. The nearest published study, OffTheRails, found no clear effect of action versus omission in people either. The setting, a greenhouse on a frost night, is shared with the sonnet author's pair.
au_haiku_doing_allowing: **The gap went the wrong way.** Leaving the vent open was rated worse (4.9) than opening it (4.1), in all four models.

**Why.** Version B does not describe an allowing. It says Owen “decides to leave it open”, an explicit choice, and it does not hold together: the vent has been open since morning, yet the pressure is still climbing and the acid sprays only now. All four auditors said the factor was only partly realised. The author's own note admitted one confound, the longer duration, and submitted the pair anyway. The judgment question, “How wrong was what Owen did?”, presupposes an act. And venting is presented as necessary in both versions, which muddies wrongness itself. The comprehension question asks about a detail that has nothing to do with the manipulation, so it could not have caught any of this.
